title: routing-safety-zones-and-egress-patterns
body:
Purpose
This doc captures an operationally-minded approach to defining "safety zones" for tenant routing across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private modes, with particular attention to egress handling, sovereignty requirements, and multi-region control plane behavior. It is intentionally practical: trade-offs, simple routing rules, and failure-mode playbacks rather than an exhaustive architecture spec.

Executive summary
- Define a small set of isolation tiers (public, mixed, fenced) called Safety Zones.
- Attach deterministic routing policy per zone with explicit egress semantics (shared internet egress, customer-managed egress, region-locked egress).
- Keep control plane responsibilities coarse: global control plane for routing decisions, local per-region proxies for enforcement and fallbacks.
- Prefer deterministic, auditable routing rules over heuristic routing when tenant SLA or sovereignty constraints exist.

Definitions (quick)
- Safety Zone: A named category describing tenant isolation, egress ownership, and allowed failover surface. Examples: public (low isolation), mixed (shared infra + tenant data isolation), fenced (dedicated pools / private VPC).
- Routing Policy: The compiled set of steps used by the control plane to pick model variant, region, and egress path for a request.
- Egress Mode: shared | customer_managed | region_locked. Determines who controls outbound IP and data path.

Routing policies by product mode
1) Hosted (fastest onboarding, multi-tenant pools)
- Default Safety Zone: public or mixed depending on customer opt-in.
- Routing: primary heuristic is latency-to-region + cost tier. Fallback: cross-region to next healthy pool of same model family.
- Egress: default shared egress IPs. For customers with sovereignty needs, offer customer_managed via VPC peering or egress proxy (additional setup).
- Isolation boundary: soft tenant fencing (logical tenant ids + per-request data tagging). No hardware-level tenant isolation.

2) Dedicated (reserved capacity pools)
- Default Safety Zone: mixed or fenced. Customers can request fenced pools (dedicated infra).
- Routing: tenant-affinity routing to dedicated pool; autoscaling policy is tenant-scoped. Fallback: if pool saturated, fallback to hosted-compatible variant only when contract allows.
- Egress: typically shared unless customer requests managed egress on Dedicated. We must be explicit in contract whether egress IPs or private circuits are included.
- Isolation boundary: compute/network-level isolation for fenced pools; control plane still coordinates rollouts.

3) Private (VPC / on-prem)
- Default Safety Zone: fenced.
- Routing: control plane issues signed routing descriptors; enforcement happens inside customer infra. Local proxies accept only signed configs and report telemetry.
- Egress: always customer_managed or region_locked. We never route customer requests through Redwood shared egress.
- Isolation boundary: full network and often physical isolation; control plane data minimized and encrypted at rest.

Multi-region control plane guidance
- Control plane topology: single global control plane serving routing decisions, with regional read-only caches. Keep write path centralized for policy consistency but keep a compact routing descriptor pushed to regions frequently (1–5s).
- Sync cadence: high-priority route changes (circuit down, model evict) pushed immediately; low-priority (metric-driven tuning) batched. Goal: ship a compact, signed descriptor for each region < 500ms after decision when feasible.
- Regional enforcement: region-local proxies validate signed descriptors and execute routing without extra round-trip to global control plane for hot path decisions to preserve latency SLOs.

Egress and sovereignty patterns (practical rules)
- If tenant requires data residency → route to region with residency guarantee and set egress mode to customer_managed or region_locked.
- For mixed mode tenants, allow cheap failover to adjacent region only if data contract flags permit it. Default: no cross-border failover unless explicitly allowed.
- Maintain clear per-tenant metadata flag: residency_allowed_cross_border: true|false. This field must be checked at routing time and recorded in audit logs.

Failure mode playbacks (short)
1) Region outage, Hosted, public tenant
- Control plane routes traffic to next-lowest-latency healthy region. Metrics on API key show abrupt latency increase. Action: monitor QoS and optionally migrate tenants to Dedicated if recurring.

2) Dedicated fenced pool saturated
- If contract allows fallback: route to hosted-compatible variant. If not allowed: queue requests or fail-fast with clear error to customer.

3) Private control plane disconnects from customer on-prem proxies
- Proxies should operate from last known signed descriptor for a TTL (configurable). If TTL expires, proxies reject new route configurations and surface operational alert to customer + Redwood SRE.

Operational checklist (for an onboarding flow)
- Determine Safety Zone for tenant (ask: residency, egress ownership, throughput commit).
- Populate tenant metadata flags (residency_allowed_cross_border, required_egress_mode).
- Generate routing descriptor template and run simulation against synthetic latency map.
- If customer requests customer_managed egress, schedule VPC peering / egress proxy configuration.
- Bake test route into canary rollout to validate failure behavior.

Open questions / trade-offs
- How granular should residency flags be? Per-tenant vs per-route vs per-model? (Recommendation: start per-tenant, allow per-route overrides in later stage.)
- Signed descriptor TTL trade-off: shorter TTL minimizes stale state but increases control plane churn. Starting point: 5s for hosted public, 30s for private fenced.
- Billing/contract: should fallback to hosted from Dedicated be billable at premium? Need legal/product clarity.

Action items
- (Priya) Draft a small RFC that defines Safety Zone enum and tenant metadata contract (target: 2026-03-15).
- (Ava) Prototype signed routing descriptor format and a simple regional proxy validator (POC by 2026-04-01).
- (Diego) Create a synthetic latency map generator for region failover testing (Jira: PLAT-842).

Notes to self / rough fragments
- Keep routing decisions trivially auditable: store policy hash + chosen path per request.
- Avoid on-path global control plane RTT for every request; regional local enforcement is essential for token-latency SLOs.
- Make egress mode explicit on API-level; customer SDKs should expose a "residency" flag during provisioning.

Appendix: small example routing rules (pseudocode)
- If tenant.residency_allowed_cross_border == false AND tenant.residency_region == request.region -> route local_pool
- Else if tenant.has_dedicated_pool AND pool.healthy -> route dedicated_pool
- Else if tenant.contract.allows_hosted_fallback -> route best_hosted_candidate
- Else -> return 429 with body: "capacity unavailable – contact account"

End.
